## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Sylvamo is the uncoated freesheet (office and printing paper) business spun off from International Paper in 2021. Across the five calls the story pivots twice.

bear_thesis: This is a shrinking commodity business printing its worst numbers since the spin, with the scoreboard removed. Uncoated freesheet demand declines roughly 3-5% a year on digitization — management's own 'real demand' framing concedes it — so every dollar of recovery must outrun a melting base. The near-term tape is guided to be ugly: first-quarter 2026 adjusted EBITDA was $29 million (a 4% margin, down from $125 million the prior quarter), adjusted earnings per share were negative $0.53, trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is just $10 million against a $74 million annual dividend bill, and management told analysts the second quarter (printing August 7) 'will look similar.' The revival thesis leans on stable input costs at exactly the wrong moment: Brent is up roughly 24% off early July on the renewed Hormuz blockade, and management had already flagged rising energy, chemicals, diesel and ocean freight for the second quarter before the latest escalation — the same cost lines that are supposed to stay tame while second-half price increases stick. Forensic quality is middling: guidance was withdrawn entirely at the cycle trough (February 2026), the earnings-beat rate is 3 of 7 quarters, 'one-off' reliability failures have now recurred in consecutive first quarters (North America in 2025, Europe and Brazil in 2026, a debarking drum unfixed until the fourth quarter), insiders show zero open-market buys against seven sells, and capital allocation bought $42 million of stock at an average of $44.74 then paused entirely in the high $30s. Europe has run below its cost of capital for three years with only a 2027 aspiration to fix it, and the board answered its largest shareholder's board exit with a poison pill within five days — a bid deterrent, not a value catalyst, until at least November 2026. If 2027 EBITDA only reaches ~$380 million because Europe keeps bleeding and inflation eats the price increases, the stock is worth low-$20s and the 'cheapness' was a value trap on a structurally shrinking base. Confirmation signals: a second-half 2026 free-cash-flow miss, any Eastover slippage or budget creep, a dividend cut, or European prices rolling over again.

The $29 million first-quarter EBITDA embeds ~$65 million of one-time, fully disclosed transition costs plus a deliberate inventory build; treating 2026 as run-rate ignores that management pre-announced this as 'a year of two halves' and has hit every self-issued quarterly EBITDA range it ever gave. (3) The unpriced wildcard: Atlas Holdings' ~21.5% economic exposure and the poison pill's November 9, 2026 expiry. forcing_function: Three dated events, none contractually binding on value. (1) August 7, 2026: the second-quarter print — a trough print by design, more likely to create the entry than the re-rate. (2) Fourth quarter 2026: the Eastover installation and 45-day outage completed and the 60,000-ton ramp beginning — the first hard evidence for the $50 million benefit and the 2027 step-up; this, plus the promised (still undated) investor day laying out the path to more than $300 million of free cash flow, is what forces estimates to roll to 2027. (3) November 9, 2026: the poison pill expires, structurally re-opening the activist and strategic-alternatives window for Atlas Holdings (~21.5% economic exposure, cooperation agreement dead since November 2025, board seats vacated). None of these is a binding payout with a fixed date and amount — the re-rating requires delivered numbers or an activist choosing to act — which is why the catalyst is classified as soft rather than hard.
valley_of_death: The next three to six months are guided to be the worst stretch of Sylvamo's public life, and the market may not look through it. August 7 brings a second-quarter print management has already said 'will look similar' to the first quarter's $29 million EBITDA, with $20 million more outage cost and continued inventory build. The third quarter adds the first full quarter without Riverdale supply. The fourth quarter concentrates more than half the year's maintenance cost plus the 45-day Eastover outage — free cash flow will be deeply negative through the installation window while the $18 million-per-quarter dividend keeps paying out against $10 million of trailing free cash flow. Layer on the live oil shock (energy, chemicals, ocean freight all rising into the second half) and a genuine tail risk emerges: if second-half price realization disappoints while transition costs run, the board could face a dividend-versus-Eastover choice, and a dividend cut would mechanically eject the yield base at the worst moment. There is no debt-maturity wall — the May 2026 refinancing pushed the 2027 maturities to 2032 — so this is an earnings-and-patience valley, not a solvency one. The stock sits 4% off its 52-week low with zero insider buying; nothing in the calendar forces a re-rating before the fourth-quarter Eastover completion evidence.
positioning_washout: The shareholder base has three fragile layers. First, the yield cohort: at ~4.8%, the $0.45 dividend is the reason a meaningful slice of the register owns a declining paper stock; trailing free cash flow of $10 million covers it 0.1 times, so any cut — even a prudent one to fund Eastover — triggers mechanical selling from income funds and dividend-screen ETFs. Second, the Atlas overhang: a shelf registration covering 6.3 million shares (about 15% of the count) for Atlas-related resale runs through August 13, 2026; Atlas has shown no sign of selling, but the registered exit path caps enthusiasm — and conversely, any Atlas add toward the pill's 15% trigger forces the board's hand. Third, the deep-value screens themselves: the name populates value screens on trailing multiples that will look worse, not better, after two more trough prints (trailing EBITDA and EPS both still falling), so quantitative value flows are more likely to rotate out than in through year-end. The washout scenario that creates the entry: a weak August 7 print plus an oil-driven second-half guide-down flushes the yield-and-value base into the mid-name's own buyback silence, toward $30-32.
moderator_conclusion: Sylvamo is a real business with a real 2027 case trading near its low, but the committee should not pay today for a recovery whose costs are being repriced upward by a war in real time. The regime overlay cuts against it twice: the house read says de-risk names whose thesis is hostage to the oil shock — Sylvamo's second-half margin inflection leans on exactly the energy, chemical and freight lines Brent's ~24% July surge inflates — and it penalizes soft, undated catalysts, which is what Sylvamo offers: an operational completion (Eastover, fourth quarter), an aspiration ($300 million of free cash flow, no date), and an activist window that merely opens (pill expiry November 9, 2026) rather than fires. The forensic picture is middling — management hits its own ranges but withdrew guidance at the trough, insiders are sellers, and the buyback bought high and paused low. The sum-of-the-parts work says roughly $42 of base value against $37.22, with $23 adverse and $54 favorable: a modest discount with two guided trough prints and a deeply negative free-cash-flow fourth quarter still ahead. That is a wait, not a buy. The specific wash-out to wait for: the August 7 print and the second-half guide commentary — if an oil-driven disappointment flushes the yield-and-value shareholder base toward $30-32, the same 2027 case offers roughly a dollar of downside protection per three of upside, with the Eastover completion and the pill expiry then sitting inside the holding window rather than beyond it.
